shortDescription: Bluetooth headphones suddenly sound muffled, mono, or like a phone call on Windows 11 or Windows 10? Windows switched them from A2DP stereo to the Hands-Free (HFP) call profile because a game, Discord, Microsoft Teams, Zoom, or a browser turned on the headset microphone. StereoKeeper is a free tray app that shows when your headphones drop into call mode, names the app that took the microphone, and brings high-quality stereo back with one click when Windows leaves them stuck there. Always stereo blocks call mode for good if you use a separate microphone, and turning it off puts Windows back exactly as it was. Works with Bluetooth headphones, earbuds, and gaming headsets. No ads, no account, no data collection, 30 languages, open source.
description:
StereoKeeper fixes Bluetooth headphones that suddenly sound muffled, tinny, mono, or like a phone call on Windows 11 and Windows 10. If your music, games, or movies lost their bass and stereo the moment you joined a voice chat, or the sound stayed bad even after the call ended, this app is for you. StereoKeeper (formerly BluetoothHandsFreeToggle) lives in the system tray, shows the real state of your headphones at a glance, and brings high-quality stereo sound back with one click.

Why Bluetooth headphones sound bad on a PC. Bluetooth headphones have two modes. A2DP plays high-quality stereo but has no microphone. The Hands-Free profile (HFP, shown in Windows as Hands-Free AG Audio or Hands-Free Telephony, with the device listed as a headset) carries the microphone but plays mono, low-quality audio made for phone calls. As soon as any app opens the headset microphone, Windows switches the headphones to Hands-Free mode: a game with voice chat such as Call of Duty or Fortnite, Discord, Microsoft Teams, Zoom, Google Meet in the browser, Steam voice chat, Xbox Game Bar, OBS Studio, or a voice assistant. Everything else you hear then sounds compressed and muffled too. And sometimes Windows does not switch back after the app lets go of the microphone.

See what is going on. The tray icon shows at a glance whether your headphones play in stereo, have dropped into call mode, or are protected by Always stereo. Click it, and the panel names the apps that are using the headset microphone right now and warns you when the headphones are the default Windows microphone, the most common reason they keep switching. Optional Windows notifications tell you the moment the sound turns mono and which app turned the microphone on.

Bring back stereo with one click. When the headphones are stuck in call mode, Bring back stereo restarts the headphone sound once, just as if you had reconnected the headphones, without changing any Windows settings. Call mode ends, the sound is stereo again, and the headset microphone keeps working for your next call. The panel shows every step live and even recovers a Bluetooth hands-free service that stopped responding.

Always stereo for gamers and anyone with a separate microphone. If you talk through a laptop, USB, or desk microphone, or do not need a microphone at all, turn on Always stereo. It turns off the Bluetooth Hands-Free profile in Windows, so no game or app can switch your headphones to call mode again: you always get full A2DP stereo with bass, detail, and positional audio in games. The switch is honest about the trade-off: while it is on, the headphones' own microphone does not work.

Safe and fully reversible. Before Always stereo changes anything, StereoKeeper remembers exactly how Windows was set up. Turn the switch off, and Windows goes back to precisely that state, with call mode allowed again. After every action the app checks the result, and the built-in help explains in plain words what each button changes and how to undo it. Windows asks for permission only when the app changes a setting; watching the headphones never needs it.

Made for gamers, streamers, remote workers, and students: players whose game audio turns flat when voice chat starts, streamers whose capture software grabbed the headset microphone, people who want music to sound right again after a Microsoft Teams or Zoom call, and anyone whose AirPods, Galaxy Buds, Sony, Bose, JBL, or Jabra headphones sound like a phone call on a Windows PC.

Light and private. StereoKeeper sits quietly in the tray with about 25 MB of memory, practically no CPU, and no graphics card use, so games keep every frame. No background service, no ads, no account, no telemetry, and no network connections: your data stays on your PC. Start with Windows, 30 interface languages picked from your Windows language, and a Copy info for the developer button that prepares a bug report with your user folder hidden.

Common questions. Why does my headset sound bad only while Discord or a game is open? Because that app is using the headset microphone, and Windows can use it only in the Hands-Free call mode; pick another microphone in that app or turn on Always stereo. Do I lose the headset microphone? Not with Bring back stereo. Only Always stereo turns it off, and only until you turn the switch off. Does StereoKeeper change my drivers or audio effects? No. It installs no drivers and no sound effects; it only restarts or switches off the Windows Bluetooth hands-free services that decide between stereo and call mode. What should I do before uninstalling? Turn Always stereo off first, so Windows is back exactly as it was.

Works on Windows 11 and Windows 10 (version 2004 or later), on x64 and Arm PCs, with Bluetooth headphones, earbuds, and headsets that use the standard Hands-Free profile, which is nearly all of them. StereoKeeper is free and open source under the MIT license, with the source code on GitHub.
